title: Knobs that remember
teaches: Recorded knob moves in a sequence, and controlled randomness

blocks.text: **The sound.** At the end of the last lesson you turned the cutoff by hand while the acid line played. Here is the line twice. In the first, the knobs stay put. In the second, the filter climbs through the bar, step by step, and snaps shut at the end, the same way every time round. Nobody's hand is on the knob.

blocks.caption: The acid line with the knobs still, then with a cutoff move recorded into the sequence

blocks.text: The second sequence remembers a knob as well as notes. Alongside the pitch, accent and slide of each step, it stores a value for the cutoff, and as it plays it turns the cutoff to that value at each step. Synths call this **modulation lanes**, **motion recording**, **automation** or **parameter locks**,[^p-locks] and it is how a sixteen-step pattern stops sounding like a loop.

A **lane** is a row of values, one per step, for one knob. The sequencer below has a lane for the cutoff under its steps: each bar is how far that step moves the cutoff away from where the knob is set, up to two octaves either way, so turning the knob by hand still moves the whole shape up or down. Drag across the lane to draw a shape, and hear the filter follow it.

blocks.caption: The sequencer with a cutoff lane. Draw on the lane below the steps.
blocks.task: Move the cutoff on four steps or more

blocks.text: On a real synth a lane is usually recorded rather than drawn. Put the sequencer into record, turn a knob while the pattern plays, and the sequencer keeps each step's value. Synths with lanes usually give each sequence a handful of them, often four, each assigned to any knob you choose: the cutoff on one, the resonance on another, the wave or the LFO's rate on a third. Some jump from one step's value to the next; others slide smoothly between them, so a recorded sweep stays smooth.

The other way to stop a loop sounding like a loop is to let it change itself, a little. Some sequencers have a pair of controls for this.[^spice-dice] **Dice** works out a new set of small changes to the pattern: a note dropped here, an octave jump there, an accent moved. **Spice** sets how many of those changes are heard, from none to all of them. Turn Spice up, then roll the Dice until you like what you hear. (On the MicroFreak, Dice is a button and the touch strip sets the Spice.)

blocks.caption: The sequencer with Spice and Dice. Add some spice and roll.
blocks.task: Roll the dice twice with some spice

blocks.text: This is randomness on a leash. Sample and hold (lesson 13) gave a new random value at every tick, forever. A dice roll stays put until you roll again, so a variation you like can be kept, and Spice can bring it in a little at a time. It is a quick way to find variations of a pattern that you would never have written.

Lanes and spice are two halves of one idea: the pattern carries more than notes. Many sequencers add more. A **probability** on each step says how often it plays at all. A **condition** plays it only every second or fourth time round. A step can be **ratcheted** into a quick burst of repeats.[^ratchet] Each turns a fixed bar into something that develops over many.

On an unfamiliar synth, the sequencer's lanes are often hidden behind a Record button and a knob turned while it plays; the dice and spice behind a pair of buttons, or a button's second job, reached by holding Shift. If a pattern seems to change the sound by itself, a lane is the likely reason. Recording over a lane replaces what was there, and every synth with lanes has some way to clear one; it is worth finding early.

Now make the climb from the start of the lesson. Draw the cutoff lane rising through the bar: lowest on the first of its four beats, higher on each beat after, and at least an octave up by the last. Play it and listen to the filter open as the bar goes on.

blocks.caption: The sequencer with an empty cutoff lane. Make the filter climb through the bar.

blocks.text: Try other shapes: a climb that drops back halfway, a single step that leaps up, or a lane that alternates high and low for a gated, stuttering sound. With a lane on the cutoff and an accent pattern, one sixteen-step bass line can carry a whole track.

blocks.caption: Five questions on lanes and dice
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: What does a modulation lane store?
choices: A value for one knob on each step
items.why: A lane is a row of values, one per step, that turns a knob as the pattern plays.

items.ask: How is a lane usually recorded on a synth?
choices: Turn the knob while the sequencer plays in record
items.why: Motion recording keeps what the knob was doing at each step.

choices: How many of the dice's changes are heard
items.why: Spice is the amount of the variation the dice worked out.

items.ask: How is a dice roll different from sample and hold?
choices: It stays the same until you roll again
It changes at every step, forever
items.why: A roll can be kept; sample and hold moves on at every tick.

items.ask: A pattern changes its sound by itself, the same way every bar. What is the likely cause?
items.why: A lane repeats exactly with the pattern; spice and random modes vary.

summary: **A sequence can remember knobs as well as notes**: modulation lanes, motion recording, automation, parameter locks.
**A lane is one value per step for one knob**, played back as the pattern plays.
**Lanes are usually recorded** by turning a knob while the sequencer records; about four per sequence is common.
**Dice works out a new set of variations**: dropped notes, octave jumps, moved accents.
**Spice sets how much of the variation is heard**, from none to all.
**A dice roll stays until you roll again**, unlike sample and hold's endless randomness.
**Probability, conditions and ratchets** are other ways a step can change from bar to bar.

p-locks.title: Motion sequences and parameter locks
p-locks.text: Early analogue sequencers such as the Moog 960 (1968) had three rows of knobs, so one row could play pitches while another stepped the filter cutoff. Digital step sequencers brought the idea back with different names: Korg called it a Motion Sequence on the Electribe (1999), and the Swedish company Elektron called it Parameter Locks on the Machinedrum (2001), where holding a step button and turning any knob locks that value to that step alone.

spice-dice.title: Spice and Dice
spice-dice.text: The names Spice and Dice come from Arturia's MicroFreak (2019) and its step sequencer, where a touch strip controls the amount of variation after a roll. Other instruments give the same idea other names: Mutable Instruments' Marbles module lets you lock a random loop in place with a Deja Vu knob, and Music Thing Modular's Turing Machine (2012) shifts random bits round a loop that only changes when you let new bits in.

ratchet.title: Ratcheting
ratchet.text: Ratcheting takes its name from Tangerine Dream's Christopher Franke, who in the 1970s wired his Moog sequencer so that selected steps were clocked at a faster subdivision, firing a burst of thirty-second notes inside a sixteenth-note pattern.
